split_question: Should schools in England be stopped from starting GCSE courses before Year 10?
angles: a firm rule on when GCSE teaching may begin
leave it to each school but publish what they do and why
change what the early years are for: attendance, reading, enrichment, wider skills
facts_for_writers: The Department for Education says persistent absence almost doubles between Years 7 and 9, rising to one in four children, and is 75% higher in secondary than primary for white working-class pupils (s1).

The department says schools should not start GCSE specifications early for large cohorts or routinely narrow options earlier, but teachers can still stretch high-achieving pupils; the page gives no consultation, cost or start date (s1).

In a survey of 810 teachers in England commissioned by the International Baccalaureate, 57% would keep GCSE preparation central and give Key Stage 3 a clearer identity, 26% want more weight on skills and character, and 14% want a separate curriculum (s2).
In the same research, 36% of pupils could see how their learning related to life beyond exams in most or all lessons, and 2% of teachers thought the current approach satisfactory (s2).
The school leaders' body ASCL said on 9 November that extra expectations on schools would need significant investment or risk diluting existing provision (s3).
